sources.entry: BLIS: A Framework for Rapidly Instantiating BLAS Functionality - Reduces a BLAS to one register-tile micro-kernel per architecture and states which loop owns which level of cache.

summary.title: BLIS: A Framework for Rapidly Instantiating BLAS Functionality
summary.one_liner: BLIS shows how level-2 and level-3 BLAS can be built on a few simple kernels, with architecture-specific micro-kernels and portable blocking code around them.
keywords: how to write a fast blas library
takeaways: Virtually all level-2 and level-3 BLAS computation can be expressed in terms of a very small set of kernels.
Only the small kernels need architecture-specific optimization; the higher-level framework code is generic ISO C99.
Adding a high-performance kernel speeds up every BLAS-like operation built on it, which is the framework's productivity argument.
The paper lists the shortcomings of the traditional BLAS: fixed storage, incomplete complex and mixed-domain support, an opaque single-layer API, and missing operations.
summary.summary: The paper introduces BLIS, a framework for building BLAS libraries by reducing level-2 and level-3 operations to a minimal set of kernels. It first reviews the history of BLAS and the DLA software stack, then lists the limits of the traditional BLAS interface: column-major-only storage, weak complex and mixed real/complex support, a single-layer API that hides kernels, and missing operations. It then sets feature goals (general storage, full complex support, exposed multi-layer APIs with kernels) and describes how generic code calls architecture-aware micro-kernels. Preliminary results are reported as competitive with OpenBLAS, ATLAS and Intel MKL. The page text provided is cut off before the detailed design and benchmark sections, so the specific cache-level loop ownership is not confirmed from this excerpt.
